az_mount_lemmon_santa_catalina_mountains.blurb: The Santa Catalina Mountains form a sky island rising directly north of Tucson, with the high point at Mount Lemmon. Crags are scattered from low desert foothills up to the pine forest near the top, so some stretch of rock is usually comfortable whatever the month. The range is mainly granite, with gneiss in places. Climbing here is split between bolted sport lines and traditional routes, plus a large amount of bouldering and a sprinkling of top-rope and aid. Grades span the full ladder, but the bulk sits between 5.9 and 5.12, with a solid supply of easier leads too. Most of the rock is reached along the Catalina Highway, while the Pusch Ridge canyons (Finger Rock, Ventana, Sabino) hold far smaller, quieter collections on the Tucson side. Summer monsoon storms and heat call for planning.

ut_southwest_utah.blurb: Southwest Utah gathers the climbing around St. George, Cedar City, Zion and Brian Head, a mix of low red-rock desert and high plateau. The variety of stone is unusual: sandstone is the main type near St. George, with basalt, limestone, and welded tuff elsewhere. Sport routes and boulder problems are about equally numerous, with a decent helping of trad. Most lines fall between 5.10 and 5.12, and moderates are present as well, while the bouldering runs from easy to hard. St. George and Zion are best in the cooler months, and the higher crags near Cedar City and Brian Head take over in summer. Sandstone here is on the soft side and needs a couple of dry days after rain.

az_mount_lemmon_catalina_highway.blurb: A single paved road winds from Tucson's northeast edge up through the Santa Catalina Mountains, passing desert, oak woodland, and finally cool pine forest. Crags are strung along its whole length, which gives you a choice of temperatures: lower walls for winter, the upper highway and summit crags when it heats up. The rock is granite with some gneiss. Sport climbing is the largest share, followed by trad, then plenty of boulders. Most grades fall from 5.8 to 5.12, peaking at 5.10 and 5.11. Lower Highway is the biggest section and leans toward sport and boulders. Bear Canyon mixes sport and trad, Windy Point is known for pinnacles and fins, and the Upper Highway has multi-pitch trad. A few alpine routes sit near the summit.

ca_yosemite_national_park.blurb: Yosemite is a granite park in the Sierra Nevada, and one of the most celebrated climbing destinations anywhere. Traditional climbing leads by a wide margin, from short crack pitches to huge multi-pitch walls, with a large amount of bouldering alongside a small amount of sport, aid, and alpine. Most free routes sit between 5.8 and 5.11, with a hard end above that. The Valley is low and holds the famous big walls; its heat and humidity make it best in spring and fall. Tuolumne Meadows is high and sub-alpine, with domes and knobby slabs, and is the summer choice. Smaller venues such as Hetch Hetchy and the southern end of the park are far quieter. Expect busy crowds in peak season.

wi_baraboo_range.blurb: The Baraboo Range is an eroded ridge of hard quartzite in south-central Wisconsin, around Baraboo and not far from Madison. Nearly all of the climbing is concentrated at Devil's Lake, where bluffs rise above a glacial lake; a handful of tiny outliers fill out the rest. Bouldering is the biggest share, followed by traditional leads, with a fair number of top-ropes and no sport climbing. The quartzite is smooth and glassy, favoring edging and technical sequences, and ratings are often called stiff. Routes run from easy to 5.12, with a very strong middle of 5.6 to 5.10, and boulder problems from V0 into the V8 range. Spring and fall bring the best conditions for most visitors.

wi_devil_s_lake.blurb: Devil's Lake sits just south of Baraboo, about 35 miles from Madison, where quartzite bluffs tower over a small lake. The East and West Bluffs hold the traditional climbs and top-ropes, divided into many numbered sections: the East Rampart is the busiest, followed by the Quarry, Potholes, and Railroad Tracks sections. A great deal of bouldering is spread through the woods and talus as well. Routes are traditionally protected, since this is not a bolt-clipping venue. The rock is hard and glassy, so edging matters more than smearing, and grades feel stiff. Moderates from 5.5 to 5.8 are plentiful, and there are many well-protected leads into the 5.10s plus harder technical lines. Boulders go from beginner problems up to V8 and beyond.
